## Proof

We evaluate
$$I \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\sin x}{1+2x^{2}+x^{4}}\,dx .$$

**Step 1. Simplify the denominator.**

$$1+2x^{2}+x^{4}=(1+x^{2})^{2},$$
so
$$I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin x}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\,dx.$$

**Step 2. Pass to a complex exponential.**

Write $\sin x=\operatorname{Im}(e^{ix})$ and set
$$J \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}\,dx,$$
so that $I=\operatorname{Im}J$.

**Step 3. Choose the contour.**

Consider $f(z)=\dfrac{e^{iz}}{(1+z^{2})^{2}}=\dfrac{e^{iz}}{(z-i)^{2}(z+i)^{2}}$ and the standard closed contour $C_{R}$ consisting of $[-R,R]$ on the real axis followed by the upper semicircle $\Gamma_{R}=\{Re^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le\pi\}$. For $R>1$ the contour encloses the double pole at $z=i$ (the pole at $z=-i$ lies in the lower half-plane).

**Step 4. Jordan's lemma / arc estimate.**

On $\Gamma_{R}$, $z=Re^{i\theta}$ with $\operatorname{Im}z=R\sin\theta\ge 0$, hence $|e^{iz}|=e^{-\operatorname{Im}z}\le 1$. Also $|1+z^{2}|\ge R^{2}-1$, so
$$\left|\int_{\Gamma_{R}} f(z)\,dz\right|\le \frac{\pi R}{(R^{2}-1)^{2}}\xrightarrow[R\to\infty]{}0.$$
Thus
$$J=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{C_{R}}f(z)\,dz.$$

**Step 5. Residue at the double pole $z=i$.**

$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=i} f(z)=\lim_{z\to i}\frac{d}{dz}\!\left[\frac{e^{iz}}{(z+i)^{2}}\right].$$

Compute the derivative:
$$\frac{d}{dz}\!\left[\frac{e^{iz}}{(z+i)^{2}}\right]=\frac{e^{iz}\bigl[i(z+i)-2\bigr]}{(z+i)^{3}}.$$

Evaluating at $z=i$: $z+i=2i$, $e^{i\cdot i}=e^{-1}$, $i(z+i)=i\cdot 2i=-2$, so the numerator bracket is $-2-2=-4$, and $(z+i)^{3}=(2i)^{3}=-8i$. Therefore
$$\operatorname{Res}_{z=i} f(z)=\frac{e^{-1}\cdot(-4)}{-8i}=\frac{1}{2ie}.$$

**Step 6. Apply the residue theorem.**

$$J=2\pi i\cdot\operatorname{Res}_{z=i} f(z)=2\pi i\cdot\frac{1}{2ie}=\frac{\pi}{e}.$$

**Step 7. Extract the imaginary part.**

Since $J=\dfrac{\pi}{e}$ is purely real,
$$I=\operatorname{Im}J=0.$$

**Consistency check (parity).** The integrand $\dfrac{\sin x}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}$ is odd ($\sin$ odd, denominator even), and it is absolutely integrable since $|\sin x|/(1+x^{2})^{2}=O(x^{-4})$. Hence the integral over the symmetric domain $(-\infty,\infty)$ vanishes, confirming $I=0$.

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin x}{1+2x^{2}+x^{4}}\,dx=0}$$
